newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Holocaust debate racked by conflict.
newsitem.headline: German Holocaust debate racked by conflict.

text.p: Plans to create Germany's first national monument to the Jews killed in the Holocaust hit fresh opposition on Friday when leading experts intended to guide a decision walked out of a debate on the memorial in disgust.

The row was emblematic of the failure of politicians, Jewish groups and critics to agree in over seven years of debate on the form or location of a monument intended as a reminder of the most traumatic episode in Germany's past.

"I beg you, do not let us talk this into the ground for the sake of German thoroughness," Lea Rosh, head of a citizens' group backing a monument, said in the last of three public debates intended to put an end to bickering over the monument.

The debates were called after the winner of a design competition -- featuring a huge gravestone the size of two football fields -- was rejected in 1995 by Chancellor Helmut Kohl and prominent members of the Jewish community.
Many of the 70 or so historians, artists, politicians and community leaders taking part accused Rosh of trying to silence opposition to the original design.

"This forum exists only to implement the earlier plan," said art historian Kathrin Hoffmann-Curtius before walking out of the meeting to loud applause. "This is the pinnacle of cynicism when opposing ideas are not even listed to."

"The more we show this intolerance the more we seem to lean toward a totalitarian way of doing things," added historian Christian Meier. "The more we do this, the more it seems to resemble the way of communicating in Hitler's time."
Two other panellists quit the forum in protest that they had not been given more time to express their views and numerous others left the room during key speeches.
The renewed acrimony made it doubtful whether the panellists would be able to provide a firm set of guidelines for Berlin's city administration to make a decision on the monument.

The series of debates has even thrown into question points that were agreed at the outset, as panellists objected to the site set aside between the Brandenburg Gate, a favourite tourist attraction, and the former site of Hitler's Chancellery.
Only the 15 million mark ($9 million) budget and the goal of a groundbreaking on January 27, 1999, the 54th anniversary of the liberation of the Auschwitz death camp, are still uncontroversial.
Rosh said many of the projects' critics were using their objections to disguise their opposition to any monument.
Ignatz Bubis, the head of Germany' Jewish community, said the location in the heart of the new government quarter had been chosen with care. "The time is ripe for a decision," he said.
